cnv-mayor-kurvers-dave.name: Dave Kurvers
cnv-mayor-kurvers-dave.text:
My policies are driven by a simple idea: a city should work for the people who live here. That means City Hall should be practical, predictable and accountable. Permits and business licences should have clear requirements and measurable timelines. Major projects should show the public what they cost, what changed and whether they delivered what was promised. City budgets should be understandable and resilient when growth slows. Growth should also improve daily life. We need housing that actually works for families, more shared public space as the City becomes denser, transportation solutions designed for North Vancouver, and parking and street policies that recognize how people really live and work. Local businesses should be able to survive and grow here. Residents should be able to move around the City without unnecessary friction. Public land should be treated as a long-term community asset. I am not interested in measuring success by how many plans, policies or studies City Hall produces. I want us to measure whether things actually work. If we don’t measure how City Hall performs, we can’t manage it or improve it.

Dave Kurvers is a North Vancouver resident, small-business owner and film and television professional with a long-standing interest in public policy and how communities work. He studied Human and Economic Geography and Business Administration at Simon Fraser University, including the forces that shape cities and regions: where people live and work, how transportation connects communities, and how public decisions influence growth. Dave has spent more than three decades working in British Columbia’s film and television industry. Today he works as a Digital Imaging Technician, a highly technical role requiring planning, coordination, problem solving and good decisions in complex, fast-moving environments. His involvement in public policy began much earlier. He volunteered on political campaigns while still in school and, in 1996, ran for the British Columbia Legislature in North Vancouver-Seymour. He later served as Policy Director for the Progressive Democratic Alliance and represented the party on Elections BC’s Election Advisory Committee. Thirty years later, Dave is again putting his name forward, this time for Mayor of the City of North Vancouver. His campaign starts with a simple question: does City Hall work as well as it should for the people it serves? Dave wants clearer requirements, predictable timelines, better coordination between departments and measurable standards for City services. Residents and businesses should know what City Hall requires, how long a decision should take, who is responsible and whether the City delivered what it promised. His other major priorities are making it possible for people to stay in North Vancouver through different stages of their lives, with more family-sized housing choices and better options for aging in place, and improving how people get around the City and the wider North Shore. His approach is practical: identify the problem, measure the results and make government work better. A city that works for the people who live here.

I’m running for mayor because I believe City Hall can work better for the people it serves. Residents and businesses should be able to understand what the City requires, know how long a decision should take, and expect departments to work together. When delays occur, the City should measure them, explain them and learn from them. The consequences of delay are real. A small business should not burn through its working capital while waiting for permits, inspections or something as routine as a backflow requirement to be resolved. A homeowner or builder should not have to carry months of mortgage and financing costs because a development permit is sitting in process. And when a new restaurant is moving into a space that was already operating as a restaurant, the City should not automatically treat the application as though the process is starting from zero. Existing approvals, infrastructure and prior use should count where they remain applicable. My own experiences dealing with municipal processes made me look much more closely at how the City operates. I began asking a simple question: are we measuring whether government is actually working well for the people who depend on it? That question extends beyond permits and City Hall. It applies to whether families can find homes with enough space, whether older residents can remain in the community, whether businesses can succeed, and whether people can move around North Vancouver efficiently. I want to bring a practical, results-focused approach to those problems: clearer requirements, published service standards, better coordination between departments, measurable outcomes and greater accountability. The goal is straightforward: make City government more predictable, more efficient and easier for residents and businesses to navigate.

cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.name: Linda Buchanan
cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.text: I have always believed communities are about people. Together, we have worked hard to build a caring, inclusive and connected city by putting people and community first. That is more important today than ever. These are challenging times, and many people are having to make difficult choices just to get ahead. We need a city that makes life easier and supports people at every stage of life. That means continuing to deliver housing that meets the needs of families, youth, and seniors who call our city home - or hope to. It means working collaboratively with other levels of government to improve transportation, and to make childcare and essential services more affordable and accessible. It means protecting our natural environment for future generations, creating parks, streets, and public spaces that bring people together and builds community, and supporting local businesses while creating opportunities for the next generation of entrepreneurs to invest here. I believe every generation should see themselves in our city's future - and know they belong. These are the values that have guided me over the past eight years, and the values I will continue to embrace as your Mayor. On October 17th, I ask for your Vote.

cnv-mayor-mcgraw-mike.name: Mike McGraw
cnv-mayor-mcgraw-mike.text: I've called North Vancouver home for most of my life. I'm frequently asked why I'm running. After a long career in business, I'm stepping away from it to serve this community again. Many people have told me their voice doesn't matter at City Hall. I think they have a point. I love this community and I have the experience and temperament to bring the leadership that this city needs to put residents and businesses at the centre of their focus. I put my employees first for thirty years running businesses, and I was recognized for my servant leadership style. I bring that same instinct to serving as strata council president today, in a mixed-use building. Before that, I served as an elected school trustee and on our library board, known as the voice of reason for listening to a room and voting on the merits. Show up. Regular Meet the Mayor events, for my full term, not just the campaign. Listen. Meaningful public input before decisions are made, not after. Lead. Pragmatic, disciplined council and community leadership - business acumen, not talk. I don't accept developer donations. City Hall shouldn't owe anyone but the residents and business owners it serves.

cnv-council-bentz-tammy.name: Tammy Bentz
cnv-council-bentz-tammy.text:
Key Principles for Tammy Bentz If elected, every decision Tammy makes at City Hall will be guided by five principles: Protect our environment while protecting residents from the impacts of climate change Build more homes while maintaining neighbourhood livability Invest wisely and respect taxpayers while promoting livable wages Make it easier to walk, cycle, take transit, or drive safely Govern openly, collaboratively, and with integrity North Vancouver can continue to grow into a more affordable, sustainable, welcoming, and resilient city. By working together with residents, businesses, Indigenous partners, and other governments, we can build a community that offers opportunity, protects what makes our city special, and delivers practical results for today’s residents and for future generations.

Tammy Bentz offers a new voice for North Vancouver City Council even though she has been a passionate advocate for her community in many areas over the past 25 years. Raising her kid with gratitude here on these unceded traditional territories of the Coast Salish people, she has volunteered on little league teams, school committees, & climate justice groups. There are no other issues if our city is on fire and no one can live here. Currently, as Faculty of BCIT's School of Business & Media, Tammy sees the importance of affordable, livable housing as well as accessible & efficient public transportation that helps to decrease our infamous "North Shore Traffic jams". Communication is her livelihood, working as a Script Supervisor in the film industry and creativity is her strong suit having an indepth background as a writer/director/producer in professional theatre since graduating from University. Tammy's also been a former co-owner of a small business and understands the challenges local businesses face. Tammy is optimistic with practical perseverance & dogged tenacity. She supports local business and knows we must balance budgets while being accountable to taxpayers. Balance is key in Tammy's approach to all issues as well as her huge emphasis on listening. She wants to hear from neighbours first so she can truly be their voice on council. She wants to work together with the community so as to benefit each of us...so everyone can thrive. As 2SLGBTQ+, Tammy also volunteers with the North Shore Pride alliance and supports collaboration. Discourse is key to any resolutinos and we can learn from what we disagree about as much as what we agree on. She's a big fan of beach walks, trail hikes, watching skateboarders/snowboarders/mountainbikers, libraries & reading, cats, and good food. She is honoured to be considered for this position so she can give back to the community that has given her so much.

We can protect the natural environment that defines our city while creating complete neighbourhoods where people of all ages can afford to live, work, and thrive. Tammy wants to listen to neighbours and bring their ideas forward to city council. She wants a community where we are all heard. Tammy's personal commitment to you If elected, Tammy will: Listen before making decisions Base policy on evidence Put long-term community interests ahead of short-term politics Keep residents informed Be accessible and accountable Work collaboratively to find practical & desirable solutions If elected, every decision Tammy makes at City Hall will be guided by five principles: Protect our environment while protecting residents from the impacts of climate change Build more homes while maintaining neighbourhood livability Invest wisely and respect taxpayers while promoting livable wages Make it easier to walk, roll, cycle, take transit, or drive safely Govern openly, collaboratively, and with integrity North Vancouver can continue to grow into a more affordable, sustainable, welcoming, and resilient city. By working together with residents, businesses, Indigenous partners, and other governments, we can build a community that offers opportunity, protects what makes our city special, and delivers practical results for today’s residents and for future generations.

cnv-council-boltenko-anna.name: Anna Boltenko
cnv-council-boltenko-anna.text:
If elected, I will commit to practical, transparent, and people-centred leadership. Every decision I make will be guided by one question: Will this improve everyday life for North Vancouver residents—today and for the next generation? 1. Make growth work for residents I will support housing choices that meet the needs of workers, families, seniors, newcomers, and future generations, while ensuring that transportation, utilities, parks, childcare, recreation, and community services keep pace. Growth should expand opportunity—not leave residents dealing with greater congestion, strained services, and infrastructure that has fallen behind. 2. Protect public trust I will advocate for earlier and more meaningful public engagement, clear explanations of costs and trade-offs, responsible spending, and regular public reporting on results. Residents deserve to know not only what Council decided, but why the decision was made and how community input influenced it. 3. Build safer, better-connected neighbourhoods I will champion safer crossings and school zones, accessible sidewalks and public spaces, reliable transit, and practical transportation planning that considers pedestrians, cyclists, drivers, seniors, families, and people with disabilities. Transportation choices should connect our community—not divide it. 4. Strengthen families, local businesses, and community life I will support recreation and community programs, children’s and youth well-being, local businesses, non-profit organizations, arts and culture, community events, and opportunities for residents of every generation to participate and belong. Strong cities are built through strong local partnerships. 5. Prepare North Vancouver for the future I will work to protect parks, natural areas, and our urban tree canopy; advance climate-resilient infrastructure and low-carbon buildings; and help create a more complete community where more people can live closer to work, services, recreation, and their daily needs. How I will deliver I will listen before deciding, ask difficult questions, work across governments and with community partners, establish measurable goals, and report back publicly on progress. When solutions require cooperation from TransLink or senior governments, I will advocate firmly rather than use jurisdiction as an excuse. My goal is a North Vancouver that grows without losing its heart—a city that works today and is ready for tomorrow. Smart Growth. Strong Communities. People First.

She holds a Master’s degree in Government and Municipal Management and completed doctoral studies in Strategic Management. For eight years, Anna has served on City advisory bodies, including six years as Chair of the Social Planning Advisory Committee. She currently serves on the Advisory Planning Commission. Anna is the co-founder of the Wonder Wonders Foundation and the North Shore Kids Festival, bringing together thousands of children, families, volunteers, schools, non-profit organizations, and local businesses. She also serves on the Board of Directors of ICF British Columbia and works internationally with leaders and organizations navigating change, strengthening decision-making, and building resilient teams. Across her civic, professional, and non-profit work, Anna has brought together government, businesses, schools, community organizations, volunteers, and residents to turn ideas into practical results. Her leadership approach is simple: listen first, build partnerships, plan responsibly, and keep people at the centre of every decision.

North Vancouver has been my home for more than 13 years. It is where I rebuilt my life, found community, and learned that local government is not abstract. Its decisions shape how safely we cross the street, how long we sit in traffic, whether families can find childcare and recreation, whether local businesses can thrive, and whether residents trust City Hall. I am running because North Vancouver is growing quickly, but growth must work in daily life. New housing must be planned together with roads, transit, utilities, parks, childcare, recreation, and community services—not years after residents begin feeling the pressure. We need attainable homes for workers, families, seniors, and newcomers, with thoughtful density in appropriate locations and stronger protection for livability, green space, and neighbourhood character. Residents also deserve meaningful engagement before major decisions are effectively settled, clear explanations of costs and trade-offs, and responsible use of every tax dollar. For eight years, I have served on City advisory bodies and continued building community between elections. Public service is not seasonal. I am running to do the work: listen carefully, ask difficult questions, bring people together, and plan beyond the next development or election cycle.

cnv-council-brun-david.name: David Brun
cnv-council-brun-david.text:
No grand promises. Three commitments: housing people can actually afford, reliable transit now, and responsible use of technology to improve services and protect public money. I will listen, ask tough questions and work with our neighbours to get things done. I will listen to residents, local businesses and community organizations, ask questions and challenge assumptions. I will work with City staff, the District of North Vancouver, TransLink and the provincial government where solutions require cooperation. I believe technology can improve services and help identify problems earlier, but it must include human oversight, privacy protection and accountability. Above all, I will ask whether decisions deliver lasting public value for the whole community. None of us has all the answers, but we can make better decisions by listening, working together and learning from the people affected.

Hello, my name is David Brun. I am a long‑time North Vancouver resident with deep family and community roots. My wife Karyn, an Education Assistant in School District 44, and I are raising our two sons, Jack and Sam. Jack has recently graduated and is exploring post‑secondary options, and Sam is currently attending Carson Graham. Many residents may have seen me around the community with my black Labrador guide dog, Nadia. I attended high school and post‑secondary institutions in North Vancouver before beginning a varied career that included small‑business ownership, real estate, and more than twenty years with TD Canada Trust, where I served as Customer Relations Manager for the Pacific Region. For the past nine years, I have been co‑founder of Gateway Navigation CCC Ltd., a social‑impact company focused on inclusion, accessibility, training, and employment. As an elected volunteer Board member and Treasurer for Cypress Gardens, I focus on sound governance supported by audited financial reporting and pragmatic decision‑making for maintenance and replacement planning, with a commitment to transparency and meaningful owner involvement. Finally, for fun and fitness my son Sam and I can be found with my fellow blind and sighted paddlers dragon boat racing on False Creek.

cnv-council-girard-angela.name: Angela Girard
cnv-council-girard-angela.text: Since 2018, it has been my privilege to serve you on Council. I initiated the City's living wage certification, expanded childcare on City lands, strengthened supports for tenants displaced by redevelopment, restored City funding for school playground upgrades and launched the Multicultural Community Festival task force. I also helped deliver the Harry Jerome Community Recreation and Silver Harbour Centres, the North Shore Neighbourhood House rebuild including affordable rental homes, the Central Lonsdale Business Improvement Area, and the City's first tree canopy target. Progress isn't guaranteed. If re-elected, I'll keep pushing for an affordable, connected, compassionate and inclusive City. I want to help deliver: A Home You Can Afford – more affordable homes, fewer barriers Childcare Close to Home – new spaces on City lands and in housing developments Less Time in Your Car – rapid transit expansion, safer streets, better bike routes Indigenous Reconciliation – true partnerships with local First Nations A City Built for Everyday Life – more local jobs, worker protections, thriving arts and culture scene A Climate Ready Livable City – more trees, cooling and protection from extreme weather Listening to You – act on the City's engagement plan and explore participatory budgeting for net parking revenue

cnv-council-heywood-guy.name: Guy Heywood
cnv-council-heywood-guy.text: I am passionate about North Vancouver and want to make it the best it can be for everyone: as a community, a place to raise families, and to live a good life. I have already served on City Council, for two terms ending when I did not run for re-election in 2014. Prior to that I served on the School Board and the NorthVan Recreation Commission. I am a volunteer at North Shore Neighbourhood House, helping people with tax returns, and at St Andrews Church delivering bread. I know many people that are struggling in our community. Better--not necessarily more expensive--government could do more to help. I am a CPA, former banker, with experience in mining, forestry, funerals and renewable energy. Today I help companies and First Nations with banking and finance challenges as an independent consultant. Some say North Vancouver is the best place to live in Canada. I believe that is true, but not because of our local governments. We who are blessed to live in a place that has so much, should work together and show the world how truly good government can be a source of pride and an example to the world.

cnv-council-izatt-ken.name: Ken Izatt
cnv-council-izatt-ken.text:
I grew up in North Vancouver and have been a city resident for over 45 years. I have raised my family here. My roots are firmly planted in North Vancouver

I am concerned with the direction the current council is taking us. I would like to be part of a new council for a positive change.

cnv-council-kolstee-jullian.name: Jullian Kolstee
cnv-council-kolstee-jullian.text:
Housing Our city should support diverse housing that allows young people, seniors, and families to stay in our community and share the same neighbourhoods. It’s not just how many units we need to build, it’s about who we are building them for. The people who live and work here should be able to choose North Vancouver as their home. This means mixed-use density in transit corridors, small-scale multi-unit gentle density in residential neighbourhoods, and increasing non-market housing and tenant protections. Transportation Our city should be easy and safe to get around for all our residents, businesses, and commuters. Our major transportation infrastructure isn’t municipal, but the city can help to develop solutions. Whatever our ride we’re all pedestrians with places to be, but we need good options to get us there. This means advocating for the expansion of Bus Rapid Transit, supporting an active transportation network, and providing those who already work here with more options to live here. Parks & Public Spaces Our city’s parks and public spaces should build community and promote wellbeing. They can provide social opportunities through recreation, gathering, and incidental encounters with neighbours. With increasing growth and density our parks and public spaces will be even more important. This means multi-functional, adaptive, and inclusive design. It is also an opportunity to engage local First Nations as partners to develop spaces that reflect the cultural heritage of the land. Accountability Our city should responsibly and transparently manage the funds that residents and businesses provide. If we can effectively promote civic literacy more people will engage with city hall proactively and positively. Council must manage difficult financial decisions with our long-term interest in mind. This means incorporating the new community engagement framework into the next council’s strategic plan, following through on the call for a public inquiry into the wastewater treatment plant, and monitoring debt servicing and the health of our reserves. Resilience Our city is increasingly vulnerable to climate change-related disruption and critical infrastructure failures. We all know what happens when one of our two crossings is compromised for hours, just imagine a week, or a month. Emergency preparedness requires redundancy to ensure our safety and security. This means mitigating climate change with more tree canopy and better drainage, reviewing our emergency management plans, and advocating for a redundant and seismically resilient crossing not for transportation, but for resilient critical infrastructure.

Hey, I’m Jullian Kolstee. We might have crossed paths in North Vancouver over the years. I went to school at Westview, Carson Graham, and Capilano University, and played youth sports with NVFC (before it was NVFC) and Capilano RFC. You may have seen myself or my students perform with Carson Graham Improv, remember me from my student leadership at Carson or Capilano, or just seen me at the Delbrook pool a few times a week. Or maybe it was when I worked at Capilano Mall, the Laserdome, Presentation House, or one of the other local institutions I’ve been through. Whether we’ve met or not, I'm a 35 year old son of immigrants from Chile and the Netherlands and a neurodivergent person living with disabilities. Public service has always been important to me, and my family. As a child my father was brain injured and my mother struggled to provide for my brother and I working odd jobs and stretching his teacher's pension. Were it not for labour unions, non-profits, public education, public health, and the volunteerism and generosity of this community, my family and I would not be here. We lost my father to COVID-19 in December of 2020. My father’s legacy as an educator in our community, particularly with indigenous peoples, set an example for me to follow throughout my life. Professionally, I’ve spent the past seven years with an international medical device manufacturer working to lead their organizational culture strategy and trying to improve the working lives of hundreds of workers. I also have more than 20 years of experience performing and teaching improvisational theatre, developing skills that allow me to communicate and connect without being cold or polished. Politically I’ve been active in the community since my youth and served three years elected to the Capilano Students Union. I was a candidate in the past two municipal elections for school board as an independent with no resources. I received an endorsement from the NVTA and increased my vote totals in those campaigns. I have supported political campaigns before, have liaised with MPs and MLAs, and have relationships with local leaders on the North Shore. My mother Maribell, my partner Sinéad, and I all continue to make our home here in the City of North Vancouver, despite the fact that we struggle to afford to live here. My family came to North Vancouver because of my father Anton’s work at Carson Graham Secondary. When he suffered a heart attack and became brain injured, the community rallied behind us by holding a benefit event, while friends and colleagues reached out and offered their personal assistance. I could list all the subsidies and bursaries I have received, or the countless volunteers who made an impact on me, but the fact is I can never repay my debt to my community. I hope you will all support my campaign to serve as councillor for the City of North Vancouver.

I’ve grown up and lived in North Vancouver all my life, and I’ve witnessed how this community has transformed. That change is only accelerating, and I believe our challenge is to grow while protecting what makes this place our home. When my family fell on hard times, this community supported us. I’ve been the beneficiary of your kindness and generosity throughout my life, and I’ve tried to serve through my civic engagement, teaching, volunteering, advocacy, and public service. North Vancouver has invested in me, and I’m here to return that investment on council. I’m running for City Council because I want to bring my experiences and skills to serving North Vancouver. I want to serve our long-term public interest as a councillor who approaches the issues that affect us most by engaging in difficult conversations, building real relationships, and drawing from diverse perspectives. Politicians often talk about young people being priced out of the communities they belong to. I am that person. I am not a talking point. I’m running for City Council because as a son of North Vancouver, I want a future here.

cnv-council-lai-max.name: Max Lai
cnv-council-lai-max.text:
I am sick and tired of political conversations devolving into rhetoric and quips. Clawing at each other's eyes, pointing fingers at perceived inaction, who should be responsible and who should we blame I want to bring a new tide of energy, enthusiasm, and drive to not only get people out to vote but to invigorate people to learn, find, and become engaged in their local politics I want politics to be about education and informative towards our community on the current, local political conversation. What progress has been made in current policies that have been brought forward, passed, and implemented to tackle our specific community issues. I want politics that engages and ensures that people like myself, who are running, distinguish their ideas rather than just following the pre-established quips, finger-pointing and talking points. I want politics that comes with a larger sense of accountability and responsibility. After all, we can’t be complacent if an informed voting base is updated on what is going on around the City. The inevitability of public service means it is expected to receive public scorn and distaste. Everyone has an opinion, everyone believes that they are right, and no one wants to be wrong. But the last time I checked, we run for the love of community, doing our best to represent our community, not just for the people who agree with us.

Graduating from Handsworth Secondary in 2012, I studied at SFU and graduated with a B.A. in political science. Through my education, I have seen the benefit of lifelong and continual learning. With the lenses of patience and open-mindedness I proactively look to find common ground. Additionally, I do my best to be aware that there is always a new perspective to consider and more to learn. I love swimming and teaching. My swimming experience as a lifeguard/instructor for ten years, our recreational facilities are vital to both our community’s mental and physical well-being. The facilities that we have in place should have the ability to both serve the present needs as well as invest into the community’s future. My teaching experience as a volunteer for Cheakamus Centre outdoor educational program, a YMCA camp leader for teen youth leadership, and as an education assistant for SD 45 means I understand the need for substantive, supportive programs to help reduce the cost of living and improve affordability. Political research has always been a passion of mine. Data driven policy is essential to make actionable and incremental positive changes within the community. I started by volunteering for Former MP Jonathan Wilkinson from Sept 2016-Dec 2016, helping compile, sort and organize data and files. I have experience on the federal NDP level volunteering as a research, data, and debate analyst for Justine Bell (2019) and Tammy Bentz (2021 and 2025). With what I’ve learned on these campaigns I aim at addressing important community issues such as Affordable Housing , Transportation Alternatives , Cost of Living , and many more. My community experience includes volunteering within the North Vancouver City and District to familiarize myself with the processes required to effectively implement change. I served on the Community Service Advisory Committee (2019-2021) for the District of North Vancouver to learn about quality of life concerns and address them by assisting non-profits within the community. In the City of North Vancouver, I serve on the Integrated Transportation Committee (2021-2023) to develop an understanding of current policy and the effects of new development on traffic flow. I also currently serve as President for my Strata Council since 2021, working with fellow homeowners and strata management when it comes to dealing with specific homeowner issus to dealing with developer issues. I would love to hear your experiences in the community and how I can support you and your family.

I was raised on the North Shore, and thus I will always want to continue living in this beautiful community. I love being able to find quality cafes where I can enjoy a nice cup of coffee in Lower Lonsdale. From the plethora of shops and restaurants, an abundant amount of green space and parks, to the diversity of different areas to visit, makes this the perfect community to live in. The cost of living has grown at such an unattainable pace that living on the North Shore for many is no longer a viable option. From unaffordable housing prices to rent usually eating half of one’s monthly budget for many working adults who wish to live on the North Shore, to our constant traffic woes, which forces many, for those who can’t live on the North Shore, to decide if the cost of travel is enough for the benefit of the work. Add on volatile gas prices, which can press into one’s transit budget, rising bus pricing for those trying to be conscientious, to those dependent on transit and growing grocery bills, the idea of wanting to live or continuing to live on the North Shore seems to be stretched farther and farther away. Politicians serve as the interface between the community we represent and the policymakers who look to improve our community. That we are the connecting piece between the staff and policy makers who make it, and the community that is affected by it. I believe the goal of any politician is to be a public resource for the community; the interface that translates what happens in the council meeting to educate and inform the public. It’s time to vote for those who understand both our current communities’ needs and can also envision and see what our future communities’ needs will be. I want to be that voice for our community. A voice that doesn’t talk down to you, but a voice that talks with you. A voice that listens, learns, and understands our current issues and uses all available information to make informed decisions that consider the present and the future. A voice that understands honesty, transparency, and accountability is a standard, not a campaign promise. I am running to be a councillor that works with and works for everyone, of all ages, so they can work, live and play on the North Shore

cnv-council-raisinghani-krishna.name: Krishna Raisinghani
cnv-council-raisinghani-krishna.text:
If elected, my goal would be a city where more people can find a home they can afford, move through their neighbourhood safely, build a local business, and understand how decisions affecting them are made. I want growth measured by more than the number of units approved. It should deliver the right homes, infrastructure and services that keep pace, welcoming public spaces, climate resilience and clear community benefits. Every major decision should also reflect sound financial judgment. That means testing assumptions, considering long-term costs and trade-offs, listening to the people affected, and making the numbers understandable. And the City should report back. Residents deserve to know what’s on track, what’s delayed, what was spent and whether a policy produced the result it promised. My goal is practical progress people can see and feel in their daily lives, shaped with the community and delivered with care.

I grew up on the North Shore. The neighbourhoods, local businesses, waterfront and trails aren’t just places on a map to me. They’re part of what makes North Vancouver feel like home. I also learned early that decisions made at City Hall eventually land on someone’s kitchen table. I carried that lesson into a career in finance and strategy, helping organizations navigate complex decisions, exercise fiscal responsibility and turn ideas into action. Today, I serve as Chair of the City’s Advisory Planning Commission, where I’ve spent the past several years listening, learning and providing thoughtful feedback about how our city grows. I bring deep North Shore roots, direct planning experience and nearly two decades of experience in strategy, finance and organizational leadership.

That means homes people can afford, with the infrastructure and services to support them. It means neighbourhoods where a child can safely walk or bike to school, where seniors can move around comfortably, and where our public spaces feel welcoming to everyone. And it means a City Hall that brings people in earlier, explains its decisions clearly, follows through on its commitments, and treats public money and public trust with care. North Vancouver helped shape who I am and the values I carry with me. Now, with the community, I want to help shape its next chapter.

cnv-council-robertson-andrew.name: Andrew Robertson
cnv-council-robertson-andrew.text:
Growth that strengthens community Housing growth needs to match our needs so that people can find a home in their community as their housing needs change. From aging seniors to new parents, everyone benefits when we can live near the friends and family that support us. To do this we must: Build the types of homes that people need Remove barriers to multi-generational housing projects Diversify rental home options Protect renters displaced by development Representation for all generations Council decisions are better when input reflects all residents and their needs. But with less free time to advocate for themselves, younger residents and working families are often under-represented in community consultation. These residents need a voice at the Council table. I know how to turn that perspective into better decisions and outcomes for everyone. To do this I will: Ensure all voices — not just the loudest — are considered in key decisions Encourage positive, respectful, and future-oriented civic discourse Support the infrastructure young families need A more affordable North Vancouver CNV's decisions impact your family's largest costs: housing and transportation. To improve affordability we can: Increase transit, car share, and safe mobility options Lower the cost of building new homes Increase non-market housing options Retain existing affordable rentals

Andrew grew up in the city and lives with his spouse, children, and retired mom in his childhood home near Ray Perrault Park. Andrew works as a medical physicist and clinical investigator at BC Cancer. He has a PhD in Physics from UBC and is a clinical instructor with the UBC Faculty of Medicine. Andrew has dedicated his career as a scientist, educator, and public sector worker to solving complex problems for people in need. He does this by collaborating to build evidence-based solutions grounded in shared values. That’s the kind of experience Council needs as it makes high-stakes decisions about how and where our city grows. Andrew has spent the last two years advocating for better housing and civic infrastructure for young families and multigenerational households in our city. His community volunteer work includes contributions to the North Shore Community Housing Action Committee and being the current President of the BC Association of Medical Physicists.

Many North Vancouverites worry there can’t be a future here for them or their loved ones due to our housing shortage. Recent growth has not produced the right homes for our families and workers, especially during life changes like downsizing due to aging, starting a family, or leaving a childhood home. This lack of attainable housing options makes people leave our community, weakens our social support networks, and is changing who can afford to call North Vancouver home. We need to grow differently. That means housing options for all generations, more ground-oriented and family-sized homes in established neighbourhoods, and housing that stays affordable long term. Our complex housing challenges deserve real solutions. As a public sector scientist and educator, I’m driven by solving hard problems for my community. I’ll bring that dedication to Council to ensure all generations of North Vancouverites see a future here in Canada’s most liveable small city.

cnv-council-shahriari-shervin.name: Shervin Shahriari
cnv-council-shahriari-shervin.text: First-term City Councillor for the City of North Vancouver seeking re-election • Has called North Vancouver home for over 40 years • Former Chair of the North Vancouver Museum & Archives Commission • Former Chair of the North Vancouver City Library Board • Author of the local history book North Vancouver’s Lonsdale Neighbourhood • Executive MBA, Project Management Professional (PMP) • 10 years as a college-level Business management Instructor • Over 30 years of business management experience in multiple industries

cnv-council-tumaneng-lailani.name: Lailani Tumaneng
cnv-council-tumaneng-lailani.text: My name is Lailani Tumaneng, and I am running for the position of Councilor to bring empowered representation and a collaborative voice to our community. North Vancouver has been my home for 32 years, and with my 26 years of experience as a Registered Nurse for Vancouver Coastal Health, I have dedicated my career to caring for others and advocating for the well-being of our community. As a Steward with BCNU and an Interim Chair for the Coastal Mountain Region, I have honed my leadership skills and developed a profound understanding of the importance of listening to diverse perspectives. I volunteered at CNV and APC committee at CNV. In October 2022, I was elected as one of the School Trustees for the City Of North Vancouver, and this taught me critical leadership skills, collaborative, diplomacy, boundary management, and collective decision making. If elected my primary goals If elected, my primary goals will focus on advocating for community safety, addressing the challenges of climate change, promoting sustainability, affordable housing & equitable governance, ensuring our decisions mirror the diverse fabric of our community. I am proud to stand for transparency, accountability, fiscal responsibility and service. Because WE ARE NORTH VANCOUVER!

cnv-council-valente-tony.name: Tony Valente
cnv-council-valente-tony.text:
I graduated from St. Thomas Aquinas Regional Secondary School and the UBC Sauder School of Business, where I earned a Bachelor of Commerce and later an MBA. Early in my career, I spent three years in Milan, Italy, working in logistics and product management for Whirlpool Europe. For nearly 20 years, I have worked on major infrastructure projects and in risk management, taking on increasingly senior leadership roles. Today, I work full-time as Senior Director, Infrastructure and Capital Projects for a BC Crown corporation, leading complex projects and managing the risks and challenges involved in delivering critical infrastructure. Serving the community in North Vancouver Since 2010, I have also dedicated my time to serving my community, first through my strata council, and subsequently through a series of advisory and committee roles with the District and City of North Vancouver. I have long been a proponent of public spaces where people can enjoy their city and streets, these are places where our community can gather, connect, and celebrate the outdoors.I was a founding member and Director of the North Van Urban Forum, a non-profit organization focused on addressing urban issues and encouraging consultation and transparency on the North Shore. The group organized Project Waterfront: North Van Design Jam to stimulate discussion and engagement with citizens about the future development of Lot 5, now the Shipyards on the Lower Lonsdale waterfront. I was also part of the branding committee that helped turn Lot 5 into what we now know as “The Shipyards.” Transportation is another one of my passions. As a former Chair of the HUB Cycling North Shore Committee, as well as through a variety of other local volunteer roles, I have worked with our community on cycling infrastructure and safety improvements for people of all ages and abilities, as well as e-bikes, ride-sharing, and other active transportation issues. My wife, Elena, our cat Oliver Spritz, and I live in Lower Lonsdale. When we’re not devoting most of our time to work and volunteering, we enjoy travelling and looking for ideas we can bring home to help make our city even better.

Our city has been recognized as the best place to live in Canada for two consecutive years. That is something to celebrate, but never take for granted. I want to build on that success and ensure North Vancouver remains a place where people can work, raise a family, age in place, and build a future. Over the next term, I will focus on what residents tell me matters most: better transit, more housing choices, a strong local economy, and more opportunities to enjoy our public spaces and community.

cnv-council-alexander-sean.name: Sean Alexander
cnv-council-alexander-sean.text: Sean Alexander Candidate for City Council, City of North Vancouver Independent Representation, Not Agendas Every four years, we vote for a new City Council. A Councillor’s job isn’t to play politics, serve interest groups, or follow slates and lobbyists, it is to represent you. When looking at slates and interest groups on municipal committees, ask yourself: Are they truly representing you, or pushing a pre-set agenda that ignores your needs and wants? You shouldn’t wake up to sudden developments in front of your house without warning. Decisions at City Hall must be made transparently and accountably. Government must work for residents of North Vancouver, not agendas. Proactive Communication & Year-Round Commitment My mandate is simple: bring people together rather than campaign on hot-button topics. Proactive transparency on City plans, projects, and bylaws isn't an extra service, it is an elected official's core job. As your City Councillor, my commitment lasts all four years: • No Surprises: Clear, upfront communication on local projects before shovels hit the ground. • Direct Access: Open channels for residents to reach Council without red tape. • Year-Round Service: Continuous door-knocking, returning phone calls, and remaining accessible. On October 17th, vote Sean Alexander for City Council.

cnv-council-back-holly.name: Holly Back
cnv-council-back-holly.text: I’m running for another term on City Council because our city is at a critical point. We’re experiencing continued growth, and with it come real challenges—from keeping our neighbourhoods safe and managing tax dollars responsibly to making smart infrastructure decisions. I’ve worked to support responsible growth that protects what we value about our community, while ensuring we don’t place unnecessary burdens on residents. I believe in accountability, transparency and making decisions that serve the long-term interests of our community—not just short-term fixes. My experience allows me to ask the right questions, advocate for responsible solutions and stay focused on what matters most to residents. It’s encouraging to see what we’ve built together and the vibrant community we continue to create—one that supports residents at every stage of life and meets a wide range of needs. It is an honour to serve this community. I’m committed to continuing this work with steady, thoughtful leadership and bringing my experience in business, education and community leadership to the role. Please visit my website to learn more about my background and priorities for the coming term.

cnv-council-bell-don.name: Don Bell
cnv-council-bell-don.text: It has been a privilege to serve my community as a member of City Council. I approach each issue before Council by listening to the public, applying independent thinking, common sense and using my experience in local government and business to seek the best possible decisions for our community. I am concerned about the high rate of development, increasing traffic congestion, lack of parking and challenges with new paid parking bylaw regulations. Safe streets, paths and sidewalks, conflicts between cars, pedestrians, cyclists and electric scooters. The need for truly affordable housing, climate change action, increased child care, protecting trees, reducing tax increases, and more effective public engagement on important issues. I’m pleased our new amazing Harry Jerome Community Recreation Centre and Silver Harbour Senior’s Centre finally opened. Personally disappointed new HJCRC doesn’t include a 50M pool and second sheet of ice for Curling or Hockey, as I had previously supported. Finally, I fully support a truly independent public inquiry about Waste Water Treatment Plant costs, reducing future financial impact on our taxpayers and review of Metro Vancouver Regional District structure. I ask for your vote to continue serving you. Please contact me by phone or email to discuss any issues.

cnv-council-cato-jeremy.name: Jeremy Cato
cnv-council-cato-jeremy.text: I grew up on a street where neighbours looked after each other — and after 40 years of asking questions for a living, I'm running for CNV Council to help this city do the same. For the past few years, I’ve spent my time reading this city’s budgets, decisions and plans — the documents behind the headlines. I found a City that can do big things, but often decides the big things before listening to the people who’ll live with them. I’m running for a way of deciding — define the goal, look at the evidence, be honest about who pays, and account for the result. That’s a Vital North Vancouver: a city where the small things work and the big decisions make sense. Where we’re serious about Safety, Economy and Family — and where Trust, Accountability and Transparency aren’t slogans, but how business gets done. I also have the experience and temperament to know that you don’t get your way by being the loudest voice. Be one prepared, reasonable vote — and build six others. One vote of seven. Bold thinking. Real results. I’d be grateful for your support. Learn more, get involved, say hello: https://www.jeremy-cato.ca/ — Jeremy

cnv-council-mcilroy-jessica.name: Jessica McIlroy
cnv-council-mcilroy-jessica.text: Jessica McIlroy has served on North Vancouver city council since being elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. Outside of council she works as a director of government relations with one of Canada’s leading national clean energy think tanks. During her time on council she has been a member of the board of directors of the North Vancouver City Library, North Van Arts Council and Lonsdale Energy, been chair of the city’s climate and environment task force, a member of the Metro Vancouver climate action and Indigenous relations committees, and the council representative on the City’s integrated transportation committee. Jessica believes strongly in collaboration and inter-governmental relations and is currently the 3rd Vice President of the Lower Mainland Local Government Association, a member of the BC Municipal Climate Leaders Council, and Vice-Chair of Climate Caucus. In 2025 Jessica was recognized for her leadership and efforts in local government climate action with a national Clean50 award. Jessica remains dedicated to serving the North Vancouver community and working to find collaborative solutions to building a City that is climate resilient, provides sustainable and effective transportation options, and aims to be inclusive and equitable.

cnv-trustee-hung-peggy.name: Peggy Hung
cnv-trustee-hung-peggy.text:
I know firsthand that education can change the trajectory of a person's life. As an immigrant who completed high school in British Columbia, I experienced firsthand how education can open doors, create opportunity, and build a foundation for a better future. My journey continued at Capilano University, followed by a Bachelor of Commerce and a Master of Business Administration. These experiences shaped my belief that every student deserves access to a high-quality public education, regardless of background or circumstance. For more than 20 years in the corporate sector, I have led teams, worked with people from diverse backgrounds, managed resources, and made decisions where accountability matters. I have learned that good leadership means listening, asking the right questions, balancing priorities, and being responsible for outcomes. It also means standing up for what is needed and making the case for the resources required to achieve the best results. If elected, I will advocate strongly for adequate and sustainable funding, fair and transparent resource allocation, and equality of opportunity across our schools. I will fight to ensure students and educators have the support they need to succeed. I am running because I know personally what education can make possible. I will listen, lead responsibly, and put students first.

I know what it means to be given a strong foundation and an opportunity to succeed. I also know that every student's path is different. Not every student starts from the same place, and not every student needs the same kind of support. ​But every student deserves the opportunity to discover what they are capable of. As a School Trustee, I want to bring together two perspectives that have shaped my life: the perspective of someone whose life was changed by a strong BC education, and the experience of a professional who understands leadership, accountability and responsible decision-making. I want to help ensure our schools have the resources they need, that students have the support and opportunities to succeed, and that we remain focused on preparing them for whatever comes next. I know personally what education can make possible. I want to help make that possibility available to every student.

cnv-trustee-wilson-antje.name: Antje Wilson
cnv-trustee-wilson-antje.text:
My work has focused on public education, infrastructure, community building, and public policy. Whether serving as Chair of the North Vancouver Board of Education or leading the BC Construction Roundtable, I believe the best decisions come from listening, respecting diverse perspectives, and working collaboratively. The North Shore has been my home for more than 24 years. Through raising my family, volunteering and serving our community, I have developed a deep appreciation for the role strong public institutions play in helping communities thrive. I currently serve on the Integrated Transportation Planning Commission and have contributed to our community in many roles, including ten years on the Ridgeway PAC and as Chair of the City of North Vancouver Social Planning Advisory Committee. I have also served on the City Advisory Planning Commission, North Vancouver Recreation Commission and Advisory Planning Commission, volunteered with Destination Imagination BC, and coached youth volleyball. These experiences have given me a strong understanding of municipal policy, planning, community engagement and the important connections between our schools and the broader community. I believe strong public education builds strong communities, and I remain committed to supporting students, staff, and families while helping prepare young people for the opportunities of tomorrow.

It has been a productive four years. During this term, students transitioned from online learning back to the classroom, and we worked in partnership with the Province, the City and District of North Vancouver, staff, families and PACs to strengthen public education across our community. Together, we delivered new or improved playgrounds at seven schools, completed two school additions, opened a new elementary school and added two artificial turf fields. We rebuilt the district’s financial reserves, supported a vibrant professional learning network for teachers and continued providing a comprehensive education grounded in literacy and numeracy, with opportunities in music, sports, the arts, Indigenous learning and the natural world. In the next term, I want to create more secondary-school pathways, with a particular focus on skilled trades and hands-on learning, while continuing to improve student learning outcomes and strengthen every student’s connection to their school and community.

cnv-trustee-azizi-manoochehr.name: Manoochehr Azizi
cnv-trustee-azizi-manoochehr.text: North Vancouver resident, registered architect, business owner, mentor, and community volunteer with more than 30 years of professional experience, including more than 12 years in Canada. My connection to education includes experience as a University Teaching Assistant from 2000 to 2002, many years of mentoring emerging professionals, and a family background in education through my mother who is a retired teacher. These experiences have given me a strong appreciation for the important role that teachers and public schools play in supporting students, families, and strong communities. Throughout my career, I have served in leadership, governance, financial oversight, project management, mentoring, and collaborative decision-making roles. My service with the Architectural Institute of British Columbia (AIBC) and the City of North Vancouver has strengthened my understanding of responsible governance, accountability, public interest, and the importance of listening to different perspectives. I am committed to bringing my professional experience, governance skills, collaborative approach, and community perspective to help Build Better Futures for North Vancouver Students.

cnv-trustee-navales-senora.name: Senora Navales
cnv-trustee-navales-senora.text: My name is Senora Navales, long time resident of City of North Vancouver, and I am running for the position of School Board Trustee. I put my name forward because I believe every child deserves to learn, grow and succeed in a safe, supportive and inclusive school environment. Our school are the heart of our community and the decisions made by the Board of Education have a direct impact to the students, families, teachers and staff. The children are the future of our community, I will bring an open mind and willingness to listen and I am committed to work with the teachers, families, educators, staff and fellow Trustees. We need to plan for the future needs of our growing community. My working experience as a Porter and Ward Aid at Lion's gate Hospital, I have been an active member of HEU, which I listen, support and advocate for my fellow workers, for safe and inclusive work place. I believe in working respectfully, towards fair and practical solutions, this has strengthen my communication and leadership skills.

cnv-trustee-neufeld-trish.name: Trish Neufeld
cnv-trustee-neufeld-trish.text: I’m running for School Trustee because because I’ve spent years volunteering in our schools, including serving as PAC Chair at Westview Elementary and previously as a Big Sister. I’ve had the opportunity to work with parents, teachers, principals and district staff. I’ve seen how much can be accomplished when people listen to each other and work toward a common goal. My career as a mortgage broker has also shaped how I approach problems. Every day I help people navigate complicated decisions. I listen to what matters to them, explain their options and help them find solutions that work. I’ve learned to ask questions, look at the details and take responsibility for the decisions I make. I don’t have all the answers but I know that good decisions start with listening to different perspectives, finding common ground and keeping students at the centre of the conversation. I would be honoured to bring that approach to the Board and advocate for our community to ensure our strategic direction aligns with our shared vision.

cnv-trustee-purugganan-ethel.name: Ethel Purugganan
cnv-trustee-purugganan-ethel.text: I am a proud indigenous of the Cordillera Autonomous Region of the Philippines, born and raised in Kalinga province. I graduated Bachelor of Arts Major in Philosophy at University of Santo Tomas and undergraduate of Law at San Beda University. We migrated in 1991. My passion on social justice and human rights have urged me to pursue Criminology in Douglas College but being new to Canada and a working student has a toll on me. I worked and earned 22 years experience in payroll, staffing and human resources in unionized setting. My commitment to you: TRANSPARENCY: I will be clear, honest, open and accessible to parents, staff and the community ACCOUNTABILITY: I will answer to the community through public hearing and independent audits STUDENT-CENTERED EDUCATION: I will put the students first to build autonomy, critical thinking and lifelong problem-solving skills SCHOOL SAFETY: I will protect students and staff from emergencies, violence and hazards Help me get the vote and I will be your positive voice and force to be reckoned with on the school board table. Your trust in my commitment and our children are my priority.

dnv-mayor-alexander-graham.name: Graham Alexander
dnv-mayor-alexander-graham.text:
Lifelong North Vancouver resident, UBC electrical engineer, hotelier, and developer. Graham Alexander brings deep infrastructure and management experience to his mayoral campaign, fighting for fiscal accountability, reduced municipal waste, and better transit.

Lifelong North Vancouver resident, UBC engineer, hotelier, and developer. Graham Alexander fights for fiscal accountability, reduced municipal waste, and transit solutions.

dnv-mayor-nieweler-stephan.name: Stephan Nieweler
dnv-mayor-nieweler-stephan.text:
We live in one of the finest places in Canada and the world, surrounded by mountains, forests, the sea and in close proximity to the opportunities of a great city. In recent years, the fine balance that has sustained this quality of life began to shift, as traffic gridlock became the norm, and our freedom to move was compromised. I knew early on that we required a bold solution, given the nature of our geography and the regional dynamics of traffic. In 2018, while completing my PhD in geography and planning at SFU, I led independent research on land use conditions along a North Shore to Burnaby rapid transit corridor, and provided evidence that the North Shore was ready for rail transit, not buses. At that time, I called on our leaders to embrace rail (not buses), push for the prioritization of this corridor at TransLink and the Province, and ensure completion in a decade . Eight years later, there has been little action – only a couple studies, a few more buses, and a botched $200m highway investment, all the while traffic conditions continue to deteriorate seven days a week. My name is Stephan Nieweler. I am a planning and transportation expert, born and raised in the District of North Vancouver , and long-committed to solving the transport challenges of the North Shore and the region. It would be my honour to earn your trust and serve as your next mayor, so that we can begin to implement a transformative vision for transportation and great neighbourhoods. I will relentlessly seek to convince all levels of government that this bold plan gives our residents and workers alternative options to move efficiently across the North Shore and to the region - by rail transit, by HOV, by express bus and by active modes. I grew up in the Upper Delbrook neighbourhood in the home my parents built in 1967, and went to Monteray, Braemar, Balmoral and Handsworth schools . I later attended Capilano College and was a member of the varsity men’s basketball team , before moving on to Simon Fraser University to complete a BA (Hons) in Urban Geography . This led me to nearly a decade of additional studies and professional work outside of BC, where I completed a Master of Science in Planning at the University of Toronto, specializing in sustainable transport planning and transit-oriented development. My career also brought me to reside in London UK, where I was involved with the London 2012 Olympic Transport Plan and to Mumbai, India , where I advised on the creation of a master transport plan for the rapidly growing metropolis. Upon my return to BC, I worked on teams that planned and designed the Canada Line and Millennium Line extension, as well as numerous rail transit projects around the world. I was later part of the Strategic Planning and Policy department of TransLink, gaining an understanding of the political dynamics that facilitate or impede projects from moving forward. While planning and transportation have been an enormous part of my life and career, I care about many issues in the community, and am very passionate about active living, sports and the arts . I still regularly hike the trails of Grouse and Fromme, run next to the Capilano and mountain bike in the Lower Seymour Conservation Area, and play basketball in a men’s league at Cap U. I also helped to raise a service dog who is now part of the team at Carson Graham school. As a former owner and operator of an iconic jazz club , I remain dedicated to supporting live music in this province, and in particular young musicians seeking an opportunity to get their chance. I believe that we are a better society when there are opportunities for all ages to find and engage in their passions beyond work and home, and I will consider this in every decision I make as Mayor. I am a local boy who went out and gained experience and leadership qualities in business, the arts, academics and professional planning in the public and private sector. I will use this wisdom to bring a unique voice to Council , while leading through respectful dialogue and continually listening to the feelings of all my constituents. Let’s move forward together and restore our quality of life in North Vancouver!

In 2018, while completing my PhD at SFU, I led independent research proving the North Shore was ready for rail transit, not more buses — and called on leaders to prioritize the corridor and get it built as rail within a decade. Eight years later, all we have to show is a couple of studies, a few more buses, and a botched $200 million highway investment — while traffic keeps getting worse, seven days a week. It would be my honour to serve as your next mayor, and finally deliver real options to move: by rail transit, by HOV, by express bus and by active modes.

dnv-mayor-zahedi-max.name: Max Zahedi
dnv-mayor-zahedi-max.text:
I will bring forward practical proposals, build Council support and report openly on results. The Mayor is one vote of seven, so every commitment says what I will propose, what Council must decide and what other governments control. Every initiative that needs municipal resources will come with a proposed budget, funding source and schedule. New work will be funded only from savings that are verified and not already committed to existing services, and from confirmed partner contributions. Grants will not be counted until approved. Where money or staff are not available, projects will be phased, reduced or deferred, and I will say so publicly.

Meet Max North Vancouver has been my home for 38 years. This is where I built my life, raised my family and became part of a community I care deeply about. The trails, the creeks and the neighbourhood shops are not talking points to me. They are where I have spent the last four decades. I am an independent candidate for Mayor of the District of North Vancouver: no party, no slate. You will find me on the ballot as Fardin Maximilian Zahedi ; Max is the name I go by. Why I am running I have watched a necessary public project, the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant, grow from a reported $700 million estimate to $3.86 billion. Residents still struggle to get a straight answer about how that happened or what it means for their bills. That is not a failure of engineering. It is a failure of reporting, oversight and accountability, and those are things a mayor can change. In my working life, a project that went that far over budget would have triggered a review, a written explanation and a change in how the next one was run. Residents deserve the same standard from the government closest to them. But this campaign is about more than one plant. It is about property taxes people can plan around, housing that matches what our infrastructure can carry, streets that are not permanently under construction, a District prepared for wildfire and earthquake, and a Municipal Hall that answers the phone. My background MBA in Global Management and a BSc in Computer Science Business owner and operator; operations manager Software engineering and business consulting Government and regulatory experience, including writing policy and procedures for a Crown corporation Served on three strata councils, managing budgets, contractors and hard decisions with neighbours Years of community and cultural leadership across the North Shore I speak English and Farsi My education in business and technology shapes how I approach public problems: understand the system, measure what it actually does, and report the result honestly, even when it is not flattering. How I will work Listen before deciding, and say publicly what was heard. Publish the numbers, including the inconvenient ones. Set service standards and be measured against them. Treat residents as the people who pay for all of this, because they are. The Mayor is one vote of seven on Council. My platform says clearly what I will propose, what Council must decide and what depends on other governments. At the first regular Council meeting, I will bring motions to launch a public commitment tracker and a wastewater fairness campaign, so you can check my progress against every promise. My priorities Fair wastewater costs Property taxes in check 1,000 affordable rental and co-op homes Traffic and park parking Infrastructure before growth Local business and childcare School safety Wildfire and emergency preparedness Read the full platform at MaxForMayor.ca . Accountability Starts Here.

The rising cost of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant raises serious questions about project oversight, public reporting and the burden placed on residents. We deserve a clear account of what happened, an independent examination of the decisions involved, and sustained advocacy for fairer costs. Residents should be able to understand how their money is being spent before problems become expensive surprises. My priorities extend beyond the treatment plant. They include property taxes people can plan around, affordable housing supported by infrastructure, better traffic and construction coordination, safer communities, and preparation for wildfire, earthquakes and other emergencies. I also want a municipal hall that answers questions, explains decisions and follows through.

dnv-council-anderson-daniel.name: Daniel Anderson
dnv-council-anderson-daniel.text:
Transparency and Accountability on the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant; Restoring Local Government Control over Zoning; Strategically-Placed Developments that Target Affordability; Traffic Solutions via Transit and Arterial Fixes

Daniel Anderson is the vice chair of the North Vancouver School Board, leading its audit committee and focusing on strengthening core learning initiatives. Dan is equally committed to accountability beyond education. As spokesperson for the North Shore Neighborhoods Alliance (NSNA) — a coalition of seven community associations — he has worked to expose the soaring costs of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant and has called for both provincial relief and an independent public inquiry under Section 764 and Section 765 of the Local Government Act. Dan is turning his attention to municipal politics because he believes our community is at a crossroads. The systems that support us all are under strain, housing is slipping further out of reach for young people, and too many local decisions are being shaped by Metro Vancouver and distant powers in Victoria. For the past four years, Dan has fought for his community: now he’s ready to bring that fight, and his experience, to council.

Daily gridlock has become normalized—but it shouldn’t be. We need better east-west connections that bypass bridge traffic, along with transit solutions that don’t get trapped in the same congestion. We must also push back against the unfair costs imposed on North Shore households by the bungled Wastewater Treatment Plant and demand meaningful reform at Metro Vancouver. Growth must be strategic and matched with infrastructure—not shoehorned into neighbourhoods that lack the roads, transit, sewage capacity and services to support it. Above all, we need responsible financial management so we can afford the infrastructure our community actually needs, from recreation centres and sewage upgrades to better transportation routes.

dnv-council-back-jordan.name: Jordan Back
dnv-council-back-jordan.text:
I’m a lifelong resident of the District of North Vancouver and have been proud to serve on District Council since 2018. I live in Lynn Valley with my wife, Signy, our two young children, Henry and Morgan, and our dog, Lola. I’ve spent more than 20 years working in advertising and media and currently work as a National Account Executive with PATTISON Outdoor Advertising. I also hold a Bachelor of Music from UBC and have remained active in music and the arts throughout my life. During my time on Council, I’ve represented the District with organizations including the North Vancouver Chamber of Commerce, the District Library Board, the Museum and Archives Commission, and Metro Vancouver’s Industrial Lands Strategy Task Force. I’m also an avid cyclist and triathlete and have completed seven IRONMAN triathlons and more than a dozen marathons. Growing up here and now raising my own family here has shaped my commitment to keeping North Vancouver livable, connected and welcoming for people at every stage of life.

I’m running for re-election because I care deeply about the community I have always called home. Growing up in the District and now raising my own family here has given me a strong connection to North Vancouver and a long-term perspective on the decisions we make today. The District is facing important challenges, including housing affordability, traffic congestion, aging recreation and community facilities, climate resilience, and the rising cost of delivering municipal services. I want to continue working on practical solutions to these issues while maintaining the qualities that make our neighbourhoods such desirable places to live. I’m particularly focused on creating a community where young people can see a future, families have more housing choices, seniors can remain connected and supported, and people have better options for getting around. I also believe residents should have meaningful opportunities to participate in local decisions and understand how and why those decisions are being made. I want to continue bringing an independent perspective to Council, listening to residents, working collaboratively with my colleagues, and focusing on practical results for the District.

dnv-council-bell-trey.name: Trey Bell
dnv-council-bell-trey.text:
Trey’s priorities; improving traffic congestion; better transit; more childcare & recreation opportunities; support for non-profits; affordable housing; responsible well planned development that doesn’t come at the expense of forests, expanding parks; & lowering tax increases.

Lifelong North Vancouver resident, community advocate & non-profit leader. I hold a BA in Political Science & Public Relations certificate. I have dedicated my career to supporting children, families, youth and seniors holding leadership positions at various N.Van organizations.

I’m running to put residents first and make North Vancouver even more livable. I’ll bring my experience in community service to Council to protect our environment, support families and seniors, tackle traffic and housing, and ensure taxpayers get value for every dollar.

dnv-council-bond-mathew.name: Mathew Bond
dnv-council-bond-mathew.text:
A District for all to thrive for generations to come. That vision has guided me since I was first elected in 2014. Our neighbours, friends and families should be able to build roots, stay connected and see their future here at every stage of life. Three values give that vision practical meaning. Belonging means supporting housing choices that let young people put down roots and established residents stay as their needs change. Choice means providing real options for housing and transportation, rather than having our lives dictated by scarcity, cost or a lack of safe alternatives. Connection means being able to reach one another, our daily needs and the natural places that make North Vancouver home. These values lead me to keep affordability and quality of life in the same conversation and judge Council decisions by how they affect daily life.

Mathew Bond is a professional engineer, community volunteer and father raising two daughters in North Vancouver. He also served two terms on District Council. His approach to public service was shaped by his parents, who built a home-renovation business during the difficult economy of the early 1980s and still run it today. Growing up around their business taught him the value of hard work, service and building something that lasts. Mathew graduated from Simon Fraser University in 2008 with a Bachelor of Applied Science in Systems Engineering and a Certificate in Sustainable Community Development. His career spans more than 15 years in the private and public sectors and includes major transportation infrastructure projects across British Columbia. In 2018, he stepped away from full-time engineering to care for his young children. During that time, he balanced parenting with consulting engineering, bicycle courier work, community volunteering and service as treasurer of the Lynn Valley Parent Participation Preschool. He returned to full-time engineering in 2022. From 2008 to 2013, Mathew served as president of the North Shore Mountain Bike Association. He helped establish a clear direction, build the team and develop partnerships that allowed a volunteer group to grow into an organization with paid staff, strong community relationships and an engaged membership. District residents elected Mathew to Council in 2014, and he served two terms through 2022. His work included transportation, major infrastructure, finance, heritage and regional housing. He advocated for affordable housing partnerships, safer active transportation and open, accountable public decision-making. These experiences taught Mathew to listen carefully, connect different parts of a problem, test assumptions, identify risks early and explain trade-offs clearly. He wants to bring that grounded way of working back to Council again.

The next Council will make decisions about affordability, infrastructure, transportation and long-term costs that will shape North Vancouver for generations. I am running to help Council make responsible decisions and keep them grounded in how they affect daily life.

dnv-council-hanson-jim.name: Jim Hanson
dnv-council-hanson-jim.text:
Jim cares that taxes will be capped to inflation, transportation and transit are addressed, and housing is managed responsibly to provide what is needed here.
